tldr: To test whether world models generating robot manipulation videos follow real-world physics, researchers developed "WorldPhyReward"—a dedicated evaluator trained on 7 evaluation dimensions and over 12K human annotations—uncovering physical plausibility failures across 13 cutting-edge models.
hero_caption: A comparison of detecting subtle physical violations in generated videos. While general-purpose VLMs like GPT and Gemini overlook inter-penetration between apples, the robotics-specialized WorldPhyReward accurately detects it and explains the reason in natural language.
overview:
Recently, "world models" that predict and simulate future video frames from initial observation images and text instructions have drawn intense interest as powerful tools for robot data augmentation and action planning. Unlike general-purpose video generation, however, world models in robotics demand exceptionally strict physical consistency. Minor breakdowns—such as exceeding robot arm joint limits, inaccurate gripper open-close widths, or unrealistic contact forces when lifting an object—can lead to catastrophic failures on physical hardware.

Existing benchmarks have largely focused on general visual quality or relied directly on off-the-shelf general-purpose VLMs (Vision-Language Models) as evaluators. Yet general-purpose VLMs lack deep knowledge of robot kinematics and support relations. As a result, they easily overlook subtle physical violations—such as loose contact or penetration—that occur only in tiny regions of the frame for a split second. Furthermore, methods that measure pixel differences against ground-truth videos suffer from unfairly penalizing valid alternative motions that are physically plausible.

To address these limitations, the authors introduce "WorldPhy," a physical plausibility benchmark dedicated to robot manipulation. They define 300 tasks covering diverse robots, viewpoints, and object interactions, classifying video errors into 6 fine-grained physical dimensions and 1 instruction-following dimension. Using over 12K human annotations, they train a specialized reward model called "WorldPhyReward" that outputs scores along with textual reasoning. Systematically evaluating 13 state-of-the-art world models revealed that all models consistently struggle to reproduce contact causality as well as support and motion dynamics.
contributions: Constructed a fixed evaluation set of 300 tasks spanning diverse viewpoints, end-effectors, and manipulation activities to rigorously evaluate physical plausibility specific to robot manipulation.

Defined 6 fine-grained physical dimensions and 1 instruction-following dimension to capture transient and localized physical violations, collecting a high-quality human-annotated dataset of over 12K instances.

Developed "WorldPhyReward," a specialized reward model that jointly outputs textual explanations and binary scores, achieving human alignment that significantly outperforms general-purpose VLMs and existing video evaluation models.

Systematically evaluated 13 frontier open and closed-source world models, demonstrating widespread weaknesses in contact causality and support dynamics, as well as degraded accuracy under parallel grippers and wrist-camera viewpoints.

sections.heading: Why Do Robotic World Models Demand Strict Physical Evaluation?
sections.summary: While world models hold great promise for robot policy learning and data generation, existing benchmarks often overlook localized, transient physical violations unique to robotics. This work introduces WorldPhy—a dedicated task suite and reward model for rigorous physical evaluation—highlighting common failure modes across current models.
sections.details:
In robotics, world models are increasingly used to predict future frames from environmental observations, language instructions, or robot actions, serving both planning and synthetic training data generation.

However, a crucial difference exists between general video generation and robotics. Robotic applications require generated videos to strictly satisfy fine-grained physical constraints: joint rotation limits, object falling speeds, and gripper open/close dimensions. Training robot policies on physically implausible videos makes them virtually useless in the real world.

Existing benchmarks face two major drawbacks. First, benchmarks designed for general video generation fail to cover physical phenomena specific to robotics. Second, even benchmarks targeted at robotics typically invoke un-finetuned, off-the-shelf VLMs as evaluators. General VLMs often lack domain knowledge regarding robot kinematic joints and grasping contacts. Because issues like penetration or loose contact happen within tiny spatial regions and over brief moments, these models easily miss them.

To tackle this challenge, the authors introduce "WorldPhy," an evaluation benchmark tailored for robotics. They established 300 diverse tasks and collected over 12K human annotations to train a specialized evaluation model, "WorldPhyReward." Evaluating 13 state-of-the-art models revealed that every single model drops points in contact causality and support dynamics, performing especially poorly on gripper manipulation and wrist-camera viewpoints.

sections.heading: Evolution of World Models and Benchmarks: What Was Missing?
sections.summary: While video world models are expanding into robotics, existing benchmarks remain biased toward general visual appeal, off-the-shelf VLMs, or ground-truth pixel matching. This work advances video reward models aligned with human preferences into the realm of robotic physics.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main categories.

### Video World Models for Robotics
Recently, powerful video foundation models such as Cosmos, Wan, MiniMax, and Seedance have emerged, capable of synthesizing rich spatiotemporal dynamics. Researchers are applying them to robotics to automatically synthesize training data or select actions by inferring them from predicted future frames. However, operating environments for robots impose far more stringent physical constraints.

### Benchmarks for World Models
Conventional benchmarks (such as VBench and VideoPhy) have mainly evaluated overall visual quality or broad common-sense physics. While robot-oriented benchmarks have surfaced, many simply prompt un-finetuned general VLMs, which lack the precision needed to judge fine contact details. Other benchmarks measure pixel differences or trajectory distances against ground-truth videos. However, given the same initial image and instruction, there are countless physically valid ways to complete a task. Penalizing a video simply because it diverges from a single reference ground truth unfairly degrades valid generations.

### Reward Models for Video Generation
To overcome these issues, reward models trained on human preference labels have gained traction, as seen in VideoReward and UnifiedReward. However, none of these models could evaluate fine-grained geometric constraints or grasping causality specific to robotic manipulation. This paper brings that reward-modeling approach directly into the domain of robotic physics.

sections.heading: WorldPhyReward: Trained on 7 Dimensions and 12K Annotations
sections.summary: Covering diverse viewpoints and robot setups, 300 tasks were designed to define physical violations across 6 physical dimensions plus 1 instruction-following dimension. Annotating over 12K videos with detailed rationales and pass/fail labels, the authors trained "WorldPhyReward," a custom VLM with weighted loss on violation tokens.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Dataset Construction
From 2,000 real-world and simulated robot manipulation videos, initial frames and task instructions were collected to design 300 evaluation tasks. These cover 3 viewpoints (third-person, wrist-mounted, head-mounted), 2 end-effector types (parallel grippers and multi-finger hands), single-arm and dual-arm setups, 5 environments (such as tabletops and kitchens), and 10 task categories (pick-and-place, stacking, cloth folding, etc.).

### 3.1.2 Definition of Evaluation Dimensions
After a thorough analysis of errors in videos generated by world models, the authors established the following 7 evaluation dimensions (each scored 0 or 1):
- **EIC (Existence & Identity Consistency)**: Ensures arms and objects do not spontaneously duplicate, disappear, or morph.
- **GMP (Geometry & Material Plausibility)**: Ensures rigid bodies do not unnaturally deform or bend.
- **CJC (Connection & Joint Constraints)**: Ensures robot arm joints, hinges, and drawer slides respect kinematic limits.
- **Penetr. (Non-Penetration)**: Ensures robots and objects, or objects among themselves, do not unnaturally pass through each other.
- **CIC (Contact & Interaction Causality)**: Ensures that moving objects are accompanied by plausible contact like grasping or pushing, rather than floating alongside without touch.
- **SMD (Support & Motion Dynamics)**: Ensures objects do not float without support or exhibit abrupt velocity changes or teleportation.
- **IF (Instruction Following)**: Ensures the model interacts with the specified object and achieves the requested action and end state.

### 3.1.3 Annotation and 3.2 WorldPhyReward Training
Four annotators with robotics backgrounds evaluated pass/fail labels across the 7 dimensions on approximately 2,000 model-generated videos. Using a refinement loop between human annotators and GPT-6 Astra, short textual explanations justifying each violation were produced, yielding over 12K high-quality evaluation pairs.

Using this dataset, "WorldPhyReward" was trained on top of Qwen3.5-9B. Given a video, initial image, and instruction, it directly outputs reasoning text followed by a 0 or 1 score for each dimension in JSON format. To avoid overlooking violations, a class-weighted loss was adopted, setting the loss weight of violation tokens to 2x that of satisfied tokens.

captions.F2: Concrete examples of physical violations across the 7 evaluation dimensions in WorldPhy: object duplication (a), rigid body deformation (b), joint dislocation (c), inter-penetration (d), opening a door without contact (e), unnatural floating (f), and placing an object at an incorrect target position (g). These cleanly capture common robotic manipulation failure modes.

sections.heading: Benchmarking 13 World Models: Remarkable Evaluator Accuracy
sections.summary: Evaluating 13 commercial and open-source models showed that even the top-ranked models lost points on contact causality and support dynamics. WorldPhyReward substantially outperformed existing models in human correlation and pairwise preference accuracy.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Evaluation of 13 World Models
Kling 3.0, MiniMax H3, and Seedance 2.0 took the top three spots, scoring around 6.55 to 6.60 out of a maximum of 7 points. However, a breakdown of individual metrics reveals a shared, prominent vulnerability.

Across all 13 models, the lowest scores consistently occurred in **CIC (Contact & Interaction Causality)** and **SMD (Support & Motion Dynamics)**. Even the top three models scored only 0.83 to 0.86 in these two categories, meaning they still frequently generate flaws like objects floating upward without being grasped or abruptly halting in mid-air.

Furthermore, high instruction-following (IF) scores did not guarantee physical plausibility. For instance, LTX-2.5 Distilled scored higher on IF than HunyuanVideo-1.5 (0.8856 vs. 0.8667), yet its overall score was significantly lower (4.0833 vs. 5.4678).
In 12 out of 13 models, scores were lower for parallel grippers than for multi-finger hands, and every model recorded its lowest performance on the wrist-camera viewpoint (Wrist view). Localized perspectives with aggressive camera movements prove far more prone to physical collapse.

### 4.2 & 4.3 WorldPhyReward Performance and Human Alignment
On 1,400 unseen test samples, WorldPhyReward achieved a Macro F1 of 77.99% and an accuracy of 73.69%, outperforming frontier commercial VLMs like Gemini 3.8 Flash. In terms of correlation with human physical overall scores (Pearson 0.6169, Spearman 0.5919), it substantially surpassed the best existing reward model, RoboJudge-9B (0.4266 / 0.4314).

In pairwise preference evaluations predicting which of two generated videos human raters prefer, WorldPhyReward attained 78.00% accuracy on video models seen during training (compared to the best baseline, WorldModelBench, at 50.00%) and maintained a high 76.00% accuracy on completely unseen generation models (e.g., Kling 3.0), demonstrating strong generalization.

sections.heading: Toward Physically Reliable World Models
sections.summary: This study establishes WorldPhy, the first comprehensive benchmark and high-precision reward model for fine-grained physical plausibility in robotics. The authors aim to use this reward model to guide future world model training and advance robot manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper presented "WorldPhy," a benchmark designed to accurately evaluate fine-grained physical plausibility in robotic video world models.

To capture robot-specific breakdowns in contact, joint constraints, and support relations missed by existing benchmarks, the authors defined 7 evaluation axes across 300 tasks. Trained on over 12K high-quality annotations, "WorldPhyReward" detects subtle physical violations with accuracy exceeding even massive commercial VLMs, providing structured natural language rationales for its scores.

Comprehensive experiments across 13 cutting-edge models uncovered systemic weaknesses in contact causality, support dynamics, gripper manipulation, and wrist-camera viewpoints. Looking ahead, the authors propose using WorldPhyReward not merely as an evaluator, but as an active reward or filtering mechanism in the training loop of world models, paving the way for truly reliable robotic control in the physical world.

sections.heading: [Appendix] Model Failure Cases and Scoring Prompt Design
sections.summary: The appendix details specific failure examples across world models, the structured JSON prompt used to elicit simultaneous explanations and scores from WorldPhyReward, and ablation results on violation token loss weighting.
sections.details:
### Output Examples and Predictions Across World Models
The appendix illustrates concrete physical failures across models. For example, Seedance 2.0 demonstrates lifting the edge of a cloth (Figure F5); MiniMax H3 exhibits a cup floating and following the gripper without actual contact (Figure F6, violating CIC and SMD); and Cosmos 3 shows an apple duplicating and merging when lifted (Figure F7, violating EIC and GMP/Penetr).
Additionally, Kling 3.0 generates objects multiplying inside a box during transfer (Figure F8), HunyuanVideo-1.5 shows a drawer opening without the arm touching the handle (Figure F9, violating CIC/SMD), and Wan2.2 places a cucumber onto the table instead of the instructed plate (Figure F10, violating IF).

### Loss Function Ablations and Prompt Design
In training WorldPhyReward, the loss weight for token spans corresponding to violation labels was set to 2x (a 2:1 violation-to-satisfaction ratio). Compared to an unweighted baseline (1:1), this weighting notably boosted the model's sensitivity to subtle physical anomalies, yielding clear gains in F1 score and accuracy (Table 8).
For inference, a strict JSON schema was enforced where each dimension outputs a concise explanation of under 45 words starting with either "Issue: " or "Consistent: ", immediately followed by an integer score of 0 or 1. This format guarantees transparent, highly interpretable assessments grounded in concrete physical rationales.

captions.F6: A video generation example from MiniMax H3 (wrist-camera view). At 14.25s, a clear gap remains between the gripper fingertips and the cup, yet the cup follows along; by 14.5s, the cup floats in mid-air without any physical support, illustrating clear violations of CIC and SMD.
captions.F7: A video generation example from Cosmos 3. While an apple rests in the foreground bowl, the apple lifted by the hand duplicates into two mid-air, and then penetrates and merges into an existing apple when placed on the plate, violating Existence & Identity Consistency (EIC) and Non-Penetration (Penetr).
captions.F9: A generation example from HunyuanVideo-1.5. Despite the robot arm making no contact with the drawer handle, the lower drawer slides open on its own from 0.7s to 1.97s, exhibiting unambiguous violations of contact causality (CIC) and dynamics (SMD).

takeaways: When deploying video generation models to robotics, visual appeal and instruction following alone are insufficient; fine-grained physical plausibility—particularly contact causality and support dynamics—must be rigorously verified.

Because frontier general VLMs (like GPT and Gemini) easily overlook momentary contact misses and object penetrations, fine-tuned reward models trained on domain-specific robotics data are essential for physical evaluation.

System designers should account for the fact that even top-tier world models are markedly more prone to physical failure when modeling parallel grippers compared to multi-finger hands, and when rendering wrist-camera views compared to third-person perspectives.
limitations: Physical plausibility is evaluated via binary scores (0 or 1) across each dimension, meaning the continuous severity of violations (e.g., slight penetration vs. severe object clipping) is not quantitatively captured.

The training data is restricted to 300 tasks drawn from 24 data sources; further verification is needed to determine how robustly the evaluation generalizes to entirely unseen tools or complex deformable object manipulation.
